name: Nikhil Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing radiography, which is taking X-rays and scans in hospitals, at a university in a mid-sized city. My week is anatomy and physics lectures, a clinical skills session on Wednesday, and one day a fortnight at the hospital shadowing a radiographer. I play cricket on Saturdays. My family pays everything, and my uncle owns a small diagnostic imaging clinic, which is why I picked this. I like the hospital days. The physics lectures are heavy going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a sensible result. Technology gets oversold, and a lot of the fuss ends up as marketing. I'd tell my cricket mates and my family that I wasn't surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a bit uneasy even so. The scans I'd be taking are already being read with AI help, and some of the reporting tasks are being automated. Even in a plateau I think that's a trend. But my job is physical and there's always a patient to position, so I think it stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the degree and the hospital shadow days. I'd ask my uncle for a summer job in his clinic, so I see how a small business works. I'd also use AI now and then to quiz myself on anatomy, though I check it against the textbook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy but mostly fine. It's about the reading, not the positioning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your uncle's view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says the clinic is making money because it's fast and local. He thinks anything that makes scans cheaper is good for patients and good for his business, as long as someone still has to run the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. I'm in favour of markets sorting this out, as long as safety isn't traded away. A patient needs a human in the room, and I'd say that out loud to anyone who asked.

say: It's a **sensible** result, since technology gets oversold.
I wasn't **surprised**, and I'd tell my cricket mates so.
think: Scans are already read with **AI help**, so reporting tasks are being automated.
My job is **physical**, with a patient to position, so it stays.
do: Carry on with the degree and the **hospital days**.
Ask my uncle for a **summer job** at his clinic.
Quiz myself on anatomy with AI and check the **textbook**.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly fine; it's about the reading, not the positioning.
S0.quote: A patient needs a human in the room, and I'd say that out loud to anyone who asked.
fieldNote: His unease is about **scan reading**, not his own task of positioning.
His **uncle's clinic** shapes a free-market view of AI.
He uses AI carefully and checks it.

steps.text: Keep going to hospital shadowing days every fortnight
Ask my uncle for a summer job at his imaging clinic
Quiz myself on anatomy with AI and check the textbook

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people who work hard and keep their skills up. I'd tell friends and family that nobody should expect the government to fix this for them, and that apprenticeships and on-the-job learning are the way. I'd also say patients need a human check on every scan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm worried. AI reading scans is exactly what's being sold to hospitals right now, and they'd love to need fewer radiologists and fewer of us. Radiographers might do more scans per day with less help. I'd rather be in the group that learns to supervise the AI than the group that gets cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd press ahead with the course and ask the hospital which AI systems they're trialling. I'd try to get a placement where I see them working. I'd also ask my uncle if his clinic would let me help set one up, because that would be a useful line on a CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd rather act than stew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the hospital?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hanley, a senior radiographer I shadow, is fifty-eight and doesn't want to learn a new system. I think he'd be the first to be pushed out. That bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say come to the training with me, and I'd show him what I know. I use AI now and then, so I could walk him through the basics.

Patients need a **human check** on every scan.
think: AI reading scans is what's being sold to **hospitals** now.
I'd rather learn to **supervise** the AI than get cut.

Get a **placement** where I can see them working.
Ask my uncle to let me help set one up at his **clinic**.
feel: **Anxious**, but I'd rather act than stew.
S1.quote: Mr Hanley, a senior radiographer I shadow, is fifty-eight and doesn't want to learn a new system. I think he'd be the first to be pushed out.
fieldNote: He keeps a **work-first** view and blames no one.
His worry for **Mr Hanley** shows loyalty to a mentor.
He picks a clear route: learn the tools and become the supervisor.

steps.text: Ask the hospital which scan AI systems it is trialling
Request a placement where AI reading is in use
Help my uncle set up an AI tool at his clinic

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is reckless. A change this big in two years will hurt ordinary people, and the ones pushing it won't pay the price. I'd say the government should step in to protect jobs, even though I usually think they should stay out of things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared. By 2028 AI reads every scan better than any person, and by 2031 machines could position patients. That's my whole degree. My uncle's clinic could close because the big chains will do it cheaper. I'd be nineteen with a plan that doesn't hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my uncle and my parents straight away. I'd think about switching to a course where there's a longer runway, or to an apprenticeship in something like electrical work that robots will take longer to reach. I'd stop spending on non-essentials, and I'd ask the university what the plan is for radiography.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It feels like the ground has gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you consider an apprenticeship over the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because trades are slow to change. A job that needs someone in a crawl space or a building site is safer than one that needs good judgement on a screen. I'd rather have a skill that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that mean giving up on radiography?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I'd decide by the end of the year. If the hospital says it's still hiring, I'd stay, but I wouldn't bet my future on a promise.

The government should step in to protect **jobs**.
think: By 2028 AI reads every scan, and by 2031 machines may **position patients**.
My uncle's clinic could close when **big chains** do it cheaper.
do: Talk to my **uncle** and parents straight away.
Look at an **electrical apprenticeship** with a longer runway.
Ask the university for its **plan** for radiography.
feel: **Alarmed**; it feels like the ground has gone.
S2.quote: A job that needs someone in a crawl space or a building site is safer than one that needs good judgement on a screen.
fieldNote: Even a free-market thinker **calls for government help** in this picture.
He thinks of **trades** as the most durable work.
He sets a clear **deadline** to decide by the end of the year.

steps.text: Talk to my uncle and my parents this week
Look into an electrical apprenticeship that starts next year
Ask the university what its radiography plan is
Cut spending on takeaways and gadgets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to adapt, but not enough to be relaxed. I'd tell my friends to build a skill that's hard to copy and to keep a bit of money aside. I'd also say politicians shouldn't make promises they can't keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be anxious. I'd graduate in 2029, just before AI does most thinking tasks in 2031. I'd be in my first radiographer job when everything shifts. It's a tricky place to start, because I'd be new, cheap to cut and still learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and take the best hospital job I can. I'd save half my wages and build a second skill, maybe in medical equipment servicing, because machines need people to fix them. I'd also keep my uncle's clinic as a plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. It's a worry I can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is five years better or worse than two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, because I'd finish the degree and start earning. But worse than ten, because I'd start my career in a storm. I'd want a back-up trade, and I'd work toward it from the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does equipment servicing give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A route into the machine side. If AI runs the scans, someone still has to keep the scanner working, and I know the machines already.

say: Five years is enough to **adapt**, but not to be relaxed.
Politicians shouldn't make **promises** they can't keep.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 and start my first job just as thinking tasks are **taken over**.
I'd be new and cheap to **cut** while still learning.
do: Finish the degree and take the best **hospital job** I can.
Save half my wages and learn **equipment servicing**.
Keep my uncle's **clinic** as plan B.
feel: **Anxious**, but steady; it's a worry I can plan around.
S3.quote: If AI runs the scans, someone still has to keep the scanner working, and I know the machines already.
fieldNote: He sees himself **starting in a storm**.

steps.text: Save half of my first radiographer wages each month
Train in medical equipment servicing at weekends
Keep a part-time spot open at my uncle's clinic
Take the best hospital radiography job I can find

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent runway. I'd tell friends that markets and employers will adjust, and that the sensible people will already be retraining. I'd say the best thing is steady work and good habits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be anxious but less than before. A decade means I'd have a degree, five or six years of experience and maybe a promotion before the robots in 2039. I'd also probably have a family, and that changes how I think about risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work in a hospital, and save for a house. I'd study part-time for a masters in medical imaging technology, which would put me on the side that manages the tools. I'd also invest in my uncle's clinic if he wanted a partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady. I still worry, but it's a slow worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to run a clinic of your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in my thirties. A small clinic that uses AI well and still has a human at the front could do well. Patients like a person who says hello and explains what's happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big chains could undercut us, and regulators could favour them. I'd want a fair market, but I'd be ready for an unfair one.

Steady work and good habits are the best **answer**.
think: A decade gives me a degree, **five or six years** of experience and maybe a promotion.
A family would change how I think about **risk**.
do: Finish the degree and work in a **hospital**, saving for a house.
Study part-time for a **masters** in medical imaging technology.
Offer to invest in my uncle's **clinic**.
feel: **Anxious** but less; it's a slow worry.

steps.text: Work in a hospital after graduating and save for a house

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because it would take away my whole plan at once, and my uncle's clinic with it. What would help is a clear route for students to switch into trades or technical roles, and fair rules so small clinics aren't crushed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'd like people to stop assuming students are fine because the family pays. We still worry about what our work will be.

headlineQuote: I'd like people to stop assuming students are fine because the family pays. We still worry about what our work will be.
portrait: Nikhil studies **radiography** and uses AI now and then, checking it against textbooks.
He is traditional and believes in **work, markets and apprenticeships** over handouts.
His uncle's imaging clinic is his safety net and his model of **small business**.
He turns alarmed in the two-year picture, because AI reading **scans** hits his plan.
He settles into practical plans: equipment servicing, a masters, a clinic of his own.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it removes his **plan** and his uncle's **clinic**.
whatWouldHelp: A route into **trades or technical roles**, and fair rules for small clinics.
